units.translation: singing to the holy maidens of nuptial beds, not of glances, a plot (the glance falls)
of a young woman — who has tasted of a man

where M and the scholiast have ἄτα [blind folly], which Hermann corrected. ἄγα [envy] is confirmed by the words that follow (135) οἴκῳ γὰρ ἐπίφθονος Αρτεμις ἁγνά [for Artemis is envious of the house, holy one].

Hesychius: ἄγαις [envyings]: Ζηλώσεσιν [with jealousies]. The codex has ἀγαῖς [with envies]. Herodianus, in Choeroboscus on Theodosius p. 329, 27, correctly has ἄγη [envy]. On Ch. 836, where Hermann wrote ἅγαν [exceedingly] (with rough breathing) for ἦταν [they were], see under φοίνιος [blood-red].
lest some envy from the gods cast a shadow over the great mouth of Troy,
for Artemis is envious of the house, holy one
(with long α: see Choeroboscus on Theodosius p. 329, 34)
with fragments of oars and with wreckage of ruins they struck.

I have restored the Doric form. Thus Heimsoeth for ἀγήνορες πρέποντες στρατοῦ δ. σ. πύλαις ἑβδόμαις προσίστανται [brave ones, conspicuous in the army, stand at the seven gates]. On the adjective ἀγηνόρειος [brave] see under ἀγανόρειος [brave].
and seven brave lords, conspicuous in the army with spear-shaking array, stand at the gates.
brave ones, conspicuous in the army, stand at the seven gates
which Athenaeus 3 p. 99 b compares with Simonides' ἀρίσταρχος Ζεύς [Zeus best ruler].
Thus ἀγκὰς ἑλεῖν [to take in the arms] and ἀγκὰς ἔχειν [to hold in the arms] in Homer.

Scholiast: τὸ ἄγκαθεν κατὰ συγκοπὴν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀνέκαθεν, τουτέστιν ἄνωθεν [ἄγκαθεν by syncope for ἀνέκαθεν, that is, from above], to which he wrongly adds ἐξ ἀρχῆς [from the beginning]. Bekker's Anecdota p. 337: ἄγκαθεν: κατὰ ἀποκοπὴν ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀνέκαθεν. οὕτως Αἰσχύλος [ἄγκαθεν: by apocope for ἀνέκαθεν. Thus Aeschylus]. Hesychius (after the gloss ἄγριαι [wild]) ἀγρίαθεν: ἀνέκαθεν. Αἰσχύλος Αγαμέμνονι [ἀγρίαθεν: from above. Aeschylus in Agamemnon]. Schmidt conjectured that it arose from Ατρει[δῶν ἄγκ]αθεν [from the arms of the Atreidae]. On the syncope ἄγκαθεν see what Schneidewin said in Philologus vol. 3 p. 118-120. On the passage Ch. 317, where the scholiast took it as μακρόθεν [from afar], see under ἀνέκαθεν [from above]. In the same place it will be discussed on Eum. 369, where Pearson rightly changed ἄγκαθεν to ἀνέκαθεν.
sit down, taking the ancient image in your arms.
sleeping on the roof (thus Schneidewin for στέγαις [with roofs]) from the arms of the Atreidae.
